The incident response course quoted the HSE review's recommendation to plan for a scenario in which all IT, all security tools and all usual communications are gone for weeks. GitLab in 2017 had a small version of this: GitLab developed GitLab on GitLab.com, so it published its incident blog post from a separate private GitLab instance, and its public monitoring dashboard collapsed under the load of users watching the outage.

Vendors are changing the platform too. In June 2025 Microsoft's Windows Resiliency Initiative announced a private preview letting antivirus and endpoint protection run in **user mode**, outside the kernel, and **quick machine recovery**, which lets Microsoft push targeted fixes to devices stuck in the Windows Recovery Environment without hands-on work.

A recovery key stored only inside the thing it recovers is not a recovery key. The same goes for admin passwords in a vault that runs on the failed platform, runbooks on the wiki that is down, and an on-call rota in the chat tool that is offline.

Draw the dependency graph of recovery itself and look for cycles. Break them with out-of-band copies (exported keys, printed runbooks, separate comms), break-glass accounts that depend on nothing in the estate, and tested access paths for every security tool you will need on the worst day.

blocks.question: Your BitLocker recovery keys are backed up to Entra ID, and admins read them in the Entra portal using accounts federated through on-premises AD FS (Active Directory Federation Services: cloud sign-in with on-premises accounts). What is the remaining single point of failure?
options: Nothing: the keys are in the cloud
The TPM chips
The federation: if AD FS or on-prem AD is down, admins cannot sign in to read the keys, unless cloud-only break-glass accounts exist
The USB drives used for recovery
blocks.explain: The keys survive, but the path to them runs through federated sign-in. Microsoft's guidance is cloud-only emergency access accounts with no dependency on federation, so the key store stays reachable when the identity provider is down.

blocks.question: Microsoft's recovery tool offered a safe mode option that could avoid typing BitLocker recovery keys. What did it need instead?
options: An account with local administrator rights on each device
Internet access on each device
A CrowdStrike license key
Nothing: it bypassed BitLocker
blocks.explain: Safe mode works on TPM-only protected devices because the TPM still unlocks the disk, but running the fix needs local admin rights. TPM+PIN devices still need the PIN or the recovery key. Nothing bypasses BitLocker; that is its purpose.

lessons.title: Crisis management: decisions, workarounds and communication

blocks.md:
An incident team fixes systems. A **crisis** is when the incident threatens the organisation itself: its customers, its money, its reputation, its licence to operate. Crisis management is the layer above incident response that makes business decisions (stop taking orders? pay penalties? switch to manual work? tell the regulator?) and speaks for the organisation.

A tiny example from Wired's account of NotPetya at Maersk in June 2017. Gates at 17 of Maersk's 76 port terminals stopped; trucks queued for miles. A freight forwarder whom Wired calls Pablo Fernández (not their real name) said that on the first day the only official email to reach them came from a Maersk staffer's Gmail account and offered no real explanation. "Maersk was like a black hole." Systems were being rebuilt; customers had no idea what to do.

What the rules ask for. NIST SP 800-34's **crisis communications plan** sets out internal and external communication procedures, provides templates for press releases, and typically designates specific individuals as the *only* authority for answering questions from the public. DORA requires financial entities (other than microenterprises) to have a **crisis management function** that, when continuity or recovery plans are activated, sets out clear procedures for internal and external crisis communications (Article 11(7)), and to keep readily accessible **records of activities** before and during the disruption (Article 11(8)): a decision log, made at the time, with who decided what and why.

The usual structure is two tiers. A small **crisis team** of senior leaders (business, legal, communications, operations, with security and IT advising) meets on a fixed rhythm and decides. The **incident or recovery teams** do the technical work and report status, impact estimates and options up. Atlassian's 2022 review describes this cadence: a core incident team met every three hours until all sites were restored.

scenes.caption: The recovery team reports facts and estimates, with confidence: what is down, what data is at risk, earliest and likely restore times.

The crisis team decides business actions against the BIA (activate the manual ordering procedure, accept SLA penalties, keep payments suspended until data integrity is confirmed) and records each decision in the log.
One voice outward. The comms lead sends approved messages through channels that still work, with a time for the next update.
Legal duties run in parallel (the risk course's breach clocks; DORA major incident reports for financial entities).
Next cycle at the agreed time, even if nothing changed: silence is what made customers call Maersk a black hole.

blocks.md: **Manual workarounds are part of the plan.** When Maersk's systems were gone, Wired reports, staff taped paper documents to shipping containers and took bookings through personal Gmail accounts, WhatsApp and Excel; one customer described booking 500 containers via WhatsApp. That worked because people improvised. A BCP turns improvisation into a procedure: paper forms ready to print, a pre-agreed messaging channel, a spreadsheet template, and the reprocessing step (lesson 3) to load it all back afterwards.

**Communication when your own channels fail.** Atlassian's review found that the deletion also removed customer contact details and site admin contacts, so affected customers could not even file support tickets, and it took days to rebuild a reliable contact list. Its conclusion: it should have communicated broadly much earlier. GitLab in 2017 chose the opposite extreme: a public live document, a YouTube stream of the recovery with about 5,000 peak viewers, and updates on Twitter; afterwards it decided to redact engineers' names in future, because not everyone would be comfortable with their name being public.

blocks.code:
import csv, io
from datetime import date

# Nightly export of who to call per customer, kept OUTSIDE production
# (a separate SaaS account and a printed copy). Synthetic data.
export = io.StringIO("""tenant,admin_email,phone,exported
t-001,ops@alpha.example,+44 20 7946 0001,2026-11-13
t-002,it@beta.example,,2026-11-13
t-003,cto@gamma.example,+1 555 0103,2026-10-02
""")
tenants_in_prod = {"t-001", "t-002", "t-003", "t-004"}
today = date(2026, 11, 14)

rows = {r["tenant"]: r for r in csv.DictReader(export)}
for t in sorted(tenants_in_prod):
    r = rows.get(t)
    if r is None:
        print(t, "MISSING from export: unreachable if production is gone")
        continue
    age = (today - date.fromisoformat(r["exported"])).days
    issues = [f"{age} days old"] if age > 2 else []
    if not r["phone"]:
        issues.append("no phone (email may be down too)")
    print(t, "OK" if not issues else "; ".join(issues))
blocks.caption: Keep who-to-call data outside production, and check it like a backup. Output: t-001 OK / t-002 no phone (email may be down too) / t-003 43 days old / t-004 MISSING from export: unreachable if production is gone.

blocks.md: Do not let the recovery team be the crisis team. Engineers in the middle of a restore should not also be negotiating with customers and drafting press statements; and executives should not be choosing which database snapshot to restore. Separate the roles, connect them with a fixed reporting rhythm.

Crisis management decides and speaks; recovery teams fix. Keep a decision log, a fixed update rhythm, one authorised voice, contact lists stored outside production, and manual workarounds written down before they are needed.

blocks.question: During a major outage your status page is hosted on the same platform that is down. What should the crisis communications plan have specified?
options: Waiting until the platform is back before saying anything
A status channel hosted independently of the affected platform, plus pre-collected out-of-band contacts
Letting each engineer post updates on their own social media
Sending updates only to the regulator
blocks.explain: Communication channels are dependencies like any other (lesson 11). An independent status page and contact lists stored outside production are what Atlassian lacked when its contact data was deleted with the sites.

blocks.question: Why does DORA ask for readily accessible records of activities during a disruption?
options: To assign blame to individuals afterwards
To replace the incident ticketing system
So that decisions and actions can be reconstructed, reviewed and reported, rather than remembered
Because regulators run the recovery
blocks.explain: Article 11(8) asks for records of activities before and during disruption events. A contemporaneous decision log supports the post-incident review (blameless, as the IR course taught), regulatory reporting and the next plan update.

lessons.title: Exercising the plan: tabletops, functional tests, failovers and chaos

blocks.md:
A plan that has never been exercised is a hypothesis. The incident response course ran a tabletop exercise; this lesson climbs the ladder from talking about a disaster to causing one on purpose, in a controlled way.

A tiny example. A team's DR plan says "fail over the database to the standby region: 30 minutes". In a tabletop everyone agrees. In a real failover test, the promotion command needs a credential only one person has, and that person is on holiday. Only the test finds that.

SP 800-34, drawing on NIST SP 800-84 (its guide to test, training and exercise programmes), separates three activities:

- **Training** teaches people their roles. SP 800-34 asks for it at least yearly, and wants staff able to execute recovery *without the plan document*, because paper and electronic copies may be unavailable in the first hours.
- **Exercises** simulate an emergency. A **tabletop** is discussion only, with no equipment deployed. A **functional exercise** has people perform their duties in a simulated operational environment (communications, notifications, equipment setup), up to a **full-scale exercise** covering every part of the plan.
- **Tests** use quantifiable metrics in an environment as close to operational as possible: can the call tree reach everyone within the time limit; what happens when power is removed from a component; how long does a restore take.

Each needs written objectives and success criteria, and a scenario that is either the worst case or the most likely incident.

DORA turns this into law for financial entities: test ICT business continuity and response and recovery plans **at least yearly** and after substantive changes to systems supporting critical or important functions; include **cyber-attack scenarios** and **switchovers** between primary infrastructure and redundant capacity, backups and redundant facilities; and test the crisis communication plans (Article 11(6)).

A switchover test is where measured RTOs come from. The timeline shows a synthetic one: the target was 60 minutes, the measurement 85, and the slowest step was not technical.

scenes.caption: Minute 0: the primary region is cut off as planned. Monitoring fires and the incident is declared in 10 minutes.
15 minutes waiting for the one person allowed to approve failover. The runbook named a role; the rota named nobody on holiday cover.
Database promotion takes 30 minutes, then traffic moves in 5 via DNS health checks (a data-plane action, as lesson 10 recommended).

Verification takes 25 minutes because nobody had defined 'working'. Measured RTO: 85 minutes against a 60-minute target. Two fixes, neither of them technology: a deputy approver and a scripted health check.

blocks.md:
**Chaos engineering** takes testing into production, continuously. The *Principles of Chaos Engineering* define it as "the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in the system's capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production". An experiment has four steps: define a measurable **steady state** (throughput, error rate, latency); hypothesise that it continues in a control group and an experimental group; introduce real-world events (servers crashing, disks failing, connections severed); and try to disprove the hypothesis by comparing the two. The principles add: vary real-world events, run in production, automate experiments to run continuously, and **minimise the blast radius**.

[Chaos Monkey](https://github.com/Netflix/chaosmonkey), an open-source tool from the streaming company Netflix, is the classic example: it randomly terminates virtual machine instances and containers in production, so that engineers build services that survive instance failure. The script below runs one such experiment on a toy service.

blocks.code:
import random

def run(instances, health_checks, requests=3000, seed=7):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    ok = 0
    for _ in range(requests):
        pool = [i for i in instances if i["up"]] if health_checks else instances
        target = rng.choice(pool)
        ok += target["up"]
    return ok / requests

def experiment(health_checks):
    # Two identical fleets measured over the same period
    control = [{"name": f"web-{n}", "up": True} for n in range(3)]
    treated = [{"name": f"web-{n}", "up": True} for n in range(3)]
    treated[1]["up"] = False                     # inject: one instance dies
    c, t = run(control, health_checks), run(treated, health_checks)
    verdict = "hypothesis holds" if t >= 0.999 else "WEAKNESS FOUND"
    print(f"health checks={health_checks}: control {c:.1%}, "
          f"one instance down {t:.1%}: {verdict}")

# Hypothesis: losing one of three instances keeps success at 99.9% or more
experiment(health_checks=False)
experiment(health_checks=True)

health checks=False: control 100.0%, one instance down 66.8%: WEAKNESS FOUND
health checks=True: control 100.0%, one instance down 100.0%: hypothesis holds
blocks.caption: Output. Without health checks the load balancer keeps sending a third of requests to the dead instance; with them, the steady state holds.

blocks.md: Exercises fail when they are rigged to pass: announced weeks ahead, run by the people who wrote the plan, on a quiet Sunday, with the expert in the room. Inject realistic constraints (a key person unavailable, the wiki down, a backup from yesterday rather than an hour ago) and record measured times, not opinions.

Climb from training to tabletop, functional exercise, full switchover test and continuous chaos experiments. Each needs objectives, success criteria and measured results; the output is a list of gaps with owners, and the measured RTO replaces the guessed one in the plan.

blocks.question: Which activity would reveal that a failover needs a credential held by only one person?
options: A tabletop exercise, because people discuss their roles
Reading the plan document carefully
Training staff on the plan's purpose
A functional exercise or switchover test where people actually perform the failover steps
blocks.explain: Discussion assumes credentials work. Only performing the steps, as in a functional exercise or test, hits the missing credential. That is the difference SP 800-34 draws between discussing roles and executing them in a simulated or real environment.

blocks.question: In a chaos experiment, why compare an experimental group against a control group instead of just watching the error rate?
options: To separate the effect of the injected failure from normal variation in traffic
Because Chaos Monkey requires two clusters
To double the blast radius
Because steady state cannot be measured otherwise
blocks.explain: The principles define the experiment as disproving the hypothesis that steady state holds in both groups. A control shows what normal looks like at the same moment, so a difference can be attributed to the injected event.

lessons.title: Regulated resilience: DORA testing, TLPT and UK impact tolerances

blocks.md:
The risk course introduced DORA (the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) and its pillars. It has applied since 17 January 2025 to banks, insurers, investment firms and other financial entities. This lesson reads the resilience parts in detail, then compares the UK's approach, because together they show where business continuity is heading: from "do you have a plan?" to "prove, with tests, that you stay within limits".

A tiny example. A bank says its payments service has an RTO of 4 hours. A supervisor asks: in which scenarios? Tested how? Including the cloud provider? With the ransomware scenario where the backups are also targeted? DORA and the UK rules turn each of those questions into a requirement.

**DORA's continuity and recovery articles:**

- **Article 11**: an ICT business continuity policy; plans that ensure continuity of critical or important functions; a BIA of exposure to severe disruptions; tests at least yearly including cyber-attack and switchover scenarios; a crisis management function; records of activities during disruptions.
- **Article 12**: backup policies stating scope and minimum frequency by criticality; restoration and recovery procedures, tested periodically; restores onto systems physically and logically segregated from the source; redundant ICT capacity (except microenterprises); RTOs and RPOs per function that meet agreed service levels "in extreme scenarios"; and integrity checks and reconciliations when recovering.

DORA's testing articles:

- **Article 24**: a risk-based digital operational resilience testing programme, run by independent testers (internal or external, free of conflicts of interest), with appropriate tests at least yearly on all systems supporting critical or important functions.
- **Article 25**: the menu of tests: vulnerability assessments and scans, open source analyses, network security assessments, gap analyses, physical security reviews, questionnaires, source code reviews where feasible, scenario-based, compatibility, performance and end-to-end testing, and penetration testing.

**TLPT** (threat-led penetration testing, Article 26): entities identified by their supervisors must run one at least every three years. It covers several or all critical or important functions, runs on **live production systems**, includes ICT third-party providers that support those functions (or pooled tests run directly with a provider), and ends with a summary of findings and remediation plans submitted to the authority, which issues an attestation. Entities that use internal testers must contract external testers every third test.

The method comes from **TIBER-EU** (Threat Intelligence-Based Ethical Red teaming), published by the European Central Bank (ECB) in May 2018 and updated in 2024 to align with DORA's technical standards on TLPT. A test moves through phases: scoping, threat intelligence on the real adversaries of that entity, red-team testing (attackers emulating those adversaries against production), blue-team reporting, and a remediation plan, closed with a test summary report and attestation.

**The UK approach: impact tolerances.** The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA, the Bank of England's regulator for banks and insurers) set out its expectations in supervisory statement SS1/21. Firms identify **important business services** (services that deliver a specific outcome to an identifiable user outside the firm, judged by what their disruption would do to financial stability, the firm's safety and soundness and, for insurers, policyholders; internal services such as payroll do not count on their own) and set an **impact tolerance** for each: "the maximum tolerable level of disruption to an important business service as measured by a length of time in addition to any other relevant metrics".

Four details of SS1/21 matter:

1. A time-based metric is mandatory; volume or value metrics (say, at least half of normal payments) may be added.
2. Tolerances assume the disruption **will happen**: firms must not consider its cause or probability when setting them.
3. Firms **map** the people, processes, technology, facilities and information behind each service (at least annually) and test that they stay within tolerance in **severe but plausible** scenarios.
4. Firms had to be able to remain within tolerances no later than **31 March 2025**; since then it is ongoing work.

An impact tolerance is the MTD idea from lesson 2, set from the harm to customers, the firm's safety and soundness, and the market, rather than from what the firm itself is willing to accept. SS1/21 also notes that sometimes the safer choice is to *suspend* a service, for example when the integrity of its data cannot be assured.

# Can "retail payments" stay within its impact tolerance in a severe but
# plausible scenario? Synthetic test results; tolerance set by the board.
TOLERANCE_H = 24          # max tolerable disruption (time-based metric)
MIN_CAPACITY = 0.5        # and at least half of normal payments by then

scenarios = {
    "primary data centre lost":         {"restore_h": 6,  "capacity": 0.8},
    "ransomware: AD + VMs encrypted":   {"restore_h": 60, "capacity": 0.3},
    "cloud provider region outage":     {"restore_h": 3,  "capacity": 1.0},
    "payment processor down (3rd pty)": {"restore_h": 30, "capacity": 0.6},
}
for name, r in scenarios.items():
    within = r["restore_h"] <= TOLERANCE_H and r["capacity"] >= MIN_CAPACITY
    print(f"{name:<34} {r['restore_h']:>3} h, {r['capacity']:.0%}: "
          f"{'within' if within else 'BREACH: remediate'}")

**Practise legally.** Everything in this course can be practised on systems you own:

- Run a continuity tabletop with CISA's free [Tabletop Exercise Packages](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/services/cisa-tabletop-exercise-packages), which include natural disasters and ransomware.
- Build a home lab database with point-in-time recovery from PostgreSQL's documentation on [continuous archiving](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/continuous-archiving.html), then delete a table on purpose and restore to the minute before, timing every step.
- Write an automated restore test for your own backups (lesson 6) and alert on the last-success timestamp.
- Read the [Principles of Chaos Engineering](https://principlesofchaos.org/) and run a small experiment on your own lab cluster; never on systems you do not own or have no written permission to test.
- Practise investigation-side skills on [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/).

DORA requires a BIA, backup and restore procedures with segregated restore systems, yearly continuity and switchover tests, a crisis function, and TLPT on production every three years for designated firms. The UK sets impact tolerances per important business service and requires proof, by severe but plausible scenario tests, that firms stay within them.

blocks.question: Under PRA SS1/21, a firm sets a short impact tolerance for its payments service, then argues it could be longer because a full data-centre loss is very unlikely. What is wrong with that argument?
options: Nothing: tolerances should reflect probability
Impact tolerances must assume the disruption occurs; cause and probability are not considered
Tolerances only apply to cyber attacks
The PRA sets the tolerance, not the firm
blocks.explain: SS1/21 says impact tolerances should be set on the assumption that a disruption will occur, without considering its cause or probability. Likelihood belongs in risk management; the tolerance is about how much harm is tolerable once it happens.

blocks.question: Which statement about DORA's threat-led penetration testing is correct?
options: It is run in a test environment so production is never at risk
It is optional for all financial entities
It is a yearly vulnerability scan
It runs on live production systems supporting critical or important functions, at least every three years for identified entities
blocks.explain: Article 26 requires identified entities to perform TLPT at least every three years on live production systems supporting critical or important functions, following the TIBER-EU-based technical standards, with risk controls to limit impact.
